extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; policymakers and historians of economic thought
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations outlining principles for evaluating trade, money, and commercial policy — critiquing bullionist notions and enumerating instruments (restraints and encouragements) used to favour a country's balance of trade. Useful for assessing the effects of tariffs, prohibitions, bounties, and colonial monopolies on national wealth and industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wealth is not identical with gold and silver
rubrics_metrics.description: Wealth frequently signifies money in common language, but true wealth consists of lands, houses, and consumable goods — not solely in gold and silver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith repeatedly warns against the popular notion that wealth = bullion; he shows how confusing money with wealth leads to mistaken policy aims (e.g., seeking to 'multiply' gold/silver rather than to increase annual produce). Examples and extended argumentation throughout the chapter explain why focusing on money obscures real national revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of bullionism / balance-of-trade fallacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The belief that a country's wealth can be increased by importing gold and silver (by running a favourable balance of trade) is a popular but erroneous notion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith examines the channels by which war expenses were met (largely by exporting commodities rather than exporting bullion) and explains how bullion circulates internationally; he argues policy should consider effects on annual produce, not just on metal flows. He treats common counterarguments and empirical examples (e.g., American and East Indies discoveries).

rubrics_metrics.name: War financing comes mainly from export of commodities, not bullion
rubrics_metrics.description: Enormous wartime expenses are chiefly defrayed by exporting British commodities (or returns purchased with them), not by exporting gold and silver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by wartime trade practices: merchants pay foreign correspondents with commodities and bills rather than shipping specie; manufactures of high value/low bulk are especially used. Smith uses historical wartime expenses as examples (expense of 1761 ~ £19,000,000) to show specie imports couldn't have covered it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bullion of the mercantile republic circulates and is not permanently lost
rubrics_metrics.description: Bullion alternately imported and exported among commercial countries functions as the money of the great mercantile republic; its movements differ from national coin but it facilitates international exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This bullion is purchased annually with commodities and re-employed abroad; in wartime its circulation shifts toward the seat of war. The point undermines mercantilist fears that exporting bullion necessarily impoverishes the nation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufactures (fine, high-value, low-bulk goods) are appropriate for long-distance trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Finer, improved manufactures — those with great value in small bulk — are most suitable for distant export and can sustain costly foreign wars without large specie exports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith contrasts manufactures with rude produce: manufactures can be exported without sending away subsistence, they support domestic employment while providing returns abroad, and they often flourish during prolonged foreign wars (with examples of British manufactures flourishing during war).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rude produce (raw agricultural goods) cannot conveniently finance prolonged foreign wars
rubrics_metrics.description: Exporting bulky agricultural produce to buy pay and provisions for armies abroad is costly and would deprive the home population of subsistence; thus raw produce is a poor medium for sustaining long foreign wars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical comparison to ancient English kings who lacked finer manufactures; Smith attributes their inability to sustain long wars to lack of easily exportable manufactures rather than lack of money per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial/civilized nations need not accumulate treasure like primitive societies
rubrics_metrics.description: Sovereigns of improved and commercial countries are less disposed and less obliged to accumulate treasuries because they can draw extraordinary aids from subjects and follow contemporary modes of expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith contrasts simple societies (where rulers accumulate treasure and practice parsimony) with commercial societies (where vanity and court splendour encourage expenditure), offering historical anecdotes about Merovingian kings and Tartar chiefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign trade confers two main benefits: moves surplus out and brings demanded goods in
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign trade carries out the surplus part of domestic produce for which there is no home demand and brings back something in return that satisfies wants and increases enjoyment; it enlarges markets and encourages division of labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith uses this as a core positive case for trade: opening external markets improves productive powers, increases annual produce, and thereby increases real revenue and wealth. He contrasts trade with mere bullion importation as a negligible part of commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening markets enables greater division of labour and higher productive power
rubrics_metrics.description: By extending markets, foreign trade allows branches of art and manufacture to specialize and reach higher perfection, increasing the productive powers of labour and the annual produce of countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith attributes large long-term gains (e.g., post-Discovery improvements) to newly opened markets; he also notes how monopolies and restraints (e.g., East India Company exclusivity) have hindered these potential gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of new markets (America, East Indies) changes division of labour and national wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Discoveries that open new markets create opportunities for new divisions of labour and improvements in art, increasing annual production and real revenue across Europe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith discusses both positive effects (expanded markets leading to larger production) and negative historical outcomes (European exploitation of America). He contrasts freer trade with exclusive monopolies that limit benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy instruments of mercantilism: two restraints and four export encouragements
rubrics_metrics.description: Mercantile system uses six principal means to increase bullion: (1) restraint on imports of goods producible at home; (2) restraint on imports from countries with an 'unfavourable' balance; and four encouragements to exportation — drawbacks, bounties, advantageous treaties, and establishment of colonies/monopolies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith enumerates and promises to examine each: restraints via high duties or prohibitions; encouragements include drawback of duties on exported home manufactures, bounties for nascent industries, preferential treaties, and colonial monopolies. He intends to assess their effects on the annual produce of industry, not just on metal flows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint type A — prohibit/import duties on goods producible at home to secure home-market monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibiting or heavily taxing imports of goods that can be produced domestically secures the monopoly of the home market for those domestic industries (e.g., banning live cattle or foreign woollens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith notes such monopolies direct labour and stock into those industries and can encourage them, but questions whether this increases general industry or the most advantageous direction for the society; he provides examples (corn duties, silk, linen) and legal prevalence in Britain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint type B — restrict imports from particular countries with 'unfavourable' balances
rubrics_metrics.description: Restraining imports from particular foreign countries perceived to cause an unfavourable balance of trade (through duties or prohibitions) is a mercantilist tool to influence the balance of trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith treats this as a distinct kind of import restraint and groups it with other mercantile measures; he challenges their presumed effect on national wealth by analyzing effects on annual produce and resource allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Export encouragement — drawbacks (rebates of duties on exported goods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawbacks return all or part of duties/excises previously paid on goods when they are exported, reducing the domestic tax burden on exported manufactures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two occasions: on home manufactures that paid duty/excise; and on imported goods liable to duty that are re-exported. Smith presents drawbacks as a common encouragement to exportation under mercantile policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Export encouragement — bounties (subsidies for favored industries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bounties are payments or subsidies to encourage certain nascent manufactures or industries thought to deserve special favour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith identifies bounties as a deliberate encouragement to export or to establish particular domestic industries sooner than they would naturally arise; he remains sceptical about long-term aggregate gains from such interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Export encouragement — advantageous treaties and colonial monopolies
rubrics_metrics.description: Advantageous treaties procure particular privileges for a nation's goods and merchants abroad; establishment of colonies often secures monopolies and exclusive markets for the mother country's goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith argues that exclusive privileges and monopolies (as with East India companies) restrict the wider benefits trade could provide by opening free markets; he contrasts free trade with monopolized colonial trade to explain differences in advantages derived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total industry limited by capital; regulations cannot increase industry beyond capital
rubrics_metrics.description: The general industry of a society cannot exceed what its capital can employ; regulations of commerce can only divert existing industry, not increase its total amount beyond capital constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith uses the relation between capital and employment to argue against protectionist attempts to 'create' industry: only saving out of revenue increases capital and thus the capacity for more industry. He reasons that policy can change allocation but not the aggregate productive capacity without more capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individuals guided by self-interest tend to allocate capital advantageously for society
rubrics_metrics.description: Private individuals, seeking their own advantage, generally choose employments of capital that best serve their local circumstances and thereby, via an 'invisible hand', promote the public interest by enlarging annual revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith notes that individuals prefer home trade when profits are equal (safer, more visible capital), tend to direct industry toward higher-value outputs, and that statesmen cannot reliably direct private capital better than individuals themselves; he uses examples of merchants converting foreign/carrying trade into home trade when profitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence of buying cheaper foreign goods over inefficient home production
rubrics_metrics.description: If a foreign country can supply a commodity cheaper than domestic production, prudence dictates buying it rather than producing it at higher cost; redirecting domestic industry toward its comparative advantages increases the exchangeable value of annual produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith compares household prudence (tailor vs shoemaker) to national prudence: specialization and trade raise overall wealth. He argues protection that forces production of more expensive domestic goods diminishes total value of the annual produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection might accelerate the emergence of an industry but not increase total wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Restraints can sometimes create a domestic manufacture sooner than it would have arisen, but this does not imply an increase in the total industry or revenue of the society — only a change in allocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith concedes some benefit in early development of an industry via protection, but stresses that the aggregate industry is constrained by capital and savings; protection often redirects resources away from more valuable uses and thus lowers exchangeable value.
